It also applied/showed half a century ago. Software is very developer dependent.

What that reveals isn't encouraging.

I think it is fair to say, the big order bits of software design quality - in general - have moved very little. Certainly less and less over the decades.

I do believe that where quality is very highly valued, there has been slow but valuable progress.

But everywhere else you look, software systems pervasively demonstrate obviously poor design.

That this may involve the unavoidable problems dealing with complex underlying systems, as much as it represents the application developer's lack of taste, isn't an excuse. It just demonstrates that poor design permeates the stack.

This is not an argument for perfection, but an observation that even slow mostly-monotonic progress has proven to be out of reach. So far.

There is a fundamental problem being unrecognized and unsolved.

I’ve personally not felt constrained by macOS, so maybe I’m not as erudite of a config wizard as I thought or because I let things like nix-darwin and home-manager do the heavy lifting. Maybe I do have more patience for configuring at the whims of others, as my nix setup breaks every major release whereas my previous personal dot files manager written in posix shell does not.

As mentioned, that had a tough sync problem. SIGSALY changed its key every 50ms. The mechanical synching of two turntables within that range was possible. That worked because the audio was being compressed pretty hard before encryption.
Delilah, which works by using a modular analog adder to add signal and key noise, would need a new analog key value for every audio sample. Probably 3KHz or so, or about 300usec. That's beyond the precision of sync which can be achieved reliably by mechanical means.

A little bit of analog buffer would help. 
It wouldn't be a problem for transistor era electronics. You need something like an analog shift register (see "bucket-brigade device"[1]) Those were not developed until the 1970s, and, for a while, appeared in guitar pedals, reverbs, and other simple audio processing devices. If you had to do that with tubes, you'd have a whole rack of tube delay line.

Fun retro electronics project for someone.

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucket-brigade_device

They have "connectors" you can configure for a variety of services, and both specific external tools and custom webhooks: https://tailscale.com/docs/aperture/integrate

I'm building a "bring your own data" layer for agentic work of all sorts, using the webhook method for now.

In the context of Aperture, I watch for agents looking for certain types/sources of data, and instead provide them with an in-tailnet API for accessing that data.

In a personal context, think email, calendar events, music playlists, fitness app records, transactions. I've also found it useful in a professional context, but I think I need to explore that a fair bit more.

It keeps credentials out of agents hands, and provides some relatively standard ways for controlling what agents can see and change.

I need a fair bit of hardening work before I try to get random folk to use it, but I might post something more here in the next week. :)
